title: The Kiev Trap
subtitle: The developing Kiev encirclement
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: German mobile forces approached from Romny and the Kremenchuk area while Soviet headquarters sought reserves and attempted to restore its threatened rear. The pincers remained separate, but the routes available for a general withdrawal were narrowing.
body:
The warning before the ring

At 14.55 on 12 September 1941, Mikhail Kirponos warned that German forces were continuing to accumulate around Romny. Until two Soviet divisions arrived, he reported, he could not oppose them there with the force required. He asked for a tank brigade. The message, preserved in the subsequent exchange between the Soviet General Staff and the Southwestern Direction, captures the developing Kiev disaster before its outcome had become irreversible in every local detail. The German pincers had not yet joined. The Southwestern Front still existed as a fighting organisation, but its commander was trying to assemble a defence behind armies already engaged along the Dnieper.[1]

The narrowing escape routes posed a problem of command and scheduling as well as distance: formations already fighting along the river would have to move without losing the ability to protect those behind them. Kiev and the river positions to its south lay west of the routes now threatened by German mobile forces. To escape, Soviet units would have to disengage, cross or move away from the river, and pass through a narrowing area east of the city. German spearheads approaching from the north and south needed to cover less ground to meet than many Soviet formations needed to cover to leave. Yet a general withdrawal was not simply a matter of ordering everyone east. It required a sequence of movements in which rearguards, artillery, hospitals, supply columns and headquarters could use the same limited roads without destroying one another’s ability to move.[2]

The Southward Offensive followed the beginning of Guderian’s turn into Ukraine. By 12 September that movement was penetrating the Soviet rear, while Kleist’s forces were breaking out from the Dnieper farther south. The present chapter concerns the interval in which this convergence was recognised but had not been stopped. It is an interval often compressed into a single sentence about Stalin refusing to abandon Kiev. The contemporary documents permit a more precise account: warnings reached Moscow, limited withdrawals were authorized, reserves were shifted, counterattacks were attempted and the instruction to hold the principal positions continued.

From the Desna to Romny

Heinz Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group was advancing south from the area reached by Army Group Centre, with XXIV Motorised Corps carrying the principal thrust and other formations protecting its increasingly extended flanks. The Desna crossings had opened the way, but they had not removed the need to secure the roads behind the leading divisions. Soviet forces around Trubchevsk and along the Sudost continued to occupy German troops. Guderian’s later account emphasises how little of his nominal strength could therefore be concentrated at the spearhead. His complaints require scrutiny as a commander’s retrospective argument, but the operational problem itself is clear: every additional kilometre south created more flank to defend.[3]

The next important obstacle was the Seym. Guderian records XXIV Corps crossing at Baturin on 9 September after the direction of the main effort had been changed toward Romny. The advance elements of the 3rd Panzer Division reached Romny on the morning of 10 September, encountering Soviet rear services. This was a specific formation’s rapid penetration after a river crossing, not proof that the entire panzer group moved forward at the same speed. Following troops and supply columns remained distributed along earlier routes. The leading detachment could reach an objective while the organisation needed to sustain and protect it was still struggling through the approaches.[3]

Soviet reporting confirms the operational significance of Romny’s loss. The Southwestern Front’s evening summary of 12 September stated that German tank groups were spreading south and southeast from the town. Its information came from several channels, including local authorities, railway officials and the NKVD. That mixture is revealing. The enemy had entered an area where reports from rear institutions were helping replace normal contact with combat formations. The information could be valuable without being complete: a railway official might know that tanks had reached a station but be unable to determine whether they were a patrol, a reinforced advance guard or the leading elements of a division.[1]

The same summary described the Soviet 40th Army as divided into two parts. It listed small surviving groups holding sectors along the Seym and reported difficulties in obtaining ammunition and food. The army’s 10th Tank Division was credited with eleven tanks and four armoured cars, but contact with it had been lost. A report that it was moving toward Romny with a railway brigade was explicitly marked as requiring verification. These qualifications are part of the evidence. They show a headquarters attempting to reconstruct the location of its own forces while the enemy was already exploiting the uncertainty between them.[1]

German success did not depend on every Soviet formation ceasing to fight. The 21st Army was still attacking on its right on 12 September, and formations around Bakhmach continued to contest the approaches. Their resistance could impose losses and delay individual German units without closing the breach farther east. Local resistance could hold a position or delay an opposing regiment while German forces elsewhere threatened the road linking that position to the rest of the front. A formation might carry out its immediate task while its communications were being cut elsewhere. The danger lay in the changing relationship between positions, not simply in the loss of fighting spirit at each position.[1]

Reported strengths make the fragmentation more tangible. The evening summary listed the 293rd Rifle Division with 150 men and six guns and the 227th with 650 men and twenty-three guns. These are the report’s figures for battered formations in the sector, not a census of every person who still belonged to their administrative establishments. Their significance is comparative: headquarters was assigning defensive tasks to units whose names concealed very small available forces. A map showing two division symbols would suggest a solidity that the accompanying report did not support. Retaining the designation allowed the command to organise surviving troops, but it did not restore the missing battalions.[1]

The southern arm of the operation

The southern movement developed from the German bridgehead near Kremenchuk. A bridgehead is more than a foothold on the opposite bank: to support a major advance it must provide space for troops to assemble, crossings through which heavy equipment can pass and routes that allow columns to disperse after crossing. Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group depended on this preparation before it could move north into the rear of the Southwestern Front. The movement was therefore not a mirror image of Guderian’s. The northern force had already travelled through several river systems; the southern force had to turn a Dnieper crossing into an operational breakthrough.[2]

Soviet commanders understood the importance of eliminating the bridgehead. Their plans for an attack on 9 September were interrupted by rain that made roads difficult and stopped wheeled transport. A contemporary report also stated that aviation could not operate. The next day’s plan called for a converging attack by four rifle divisions, cavalry and the 3rd and 142nd Tank Brigades against the German grouping north of Prishib. These were serious attempts to contest the crossing area. They also demonstrate why the presence of several formations in an order must not be confused with their ability to attack together at the required time.[1]

By 12 September the Soviet effort had failed to restore the river line. The front’s summary reported limited initial gains by the left group of the 38th Army followed by German counterattacks and a return to the starting positions. A new directive ordered that attack stopped and the ground held, with the two tank brigades gathered near Kobelyaky for counterattacks. Meanwhile, farther toward the northern part of the army’s sector, German tanks had broken through the 297th Rifle Division and were advancing toward Hlobyne. The threat was becoming wider than the area in which Soviet commanders had assembled their counterstroke.[1]

The reported breakthrough can be followed without pretending that the Soviet headquarters possessed a complete enemy order of battle. Its evening account placed a group of German tanks through the 297th Division’s front at 14.00 and at Babychivka by 16.00. Additional reports came from reconnaissance and the railway commandant at Romodan. These were sightings of moving groups, not a continuous trace of every German unit. What mattered operationally was that roads leading into the army’s rear were becoming exposed. The Soviet command had to respond before the size and destination of each column could be established with certainty.[1]

Budenny’s headquarters also recognised a problem of command span. On 12 September it proposed dividing the 38th Army because its approximately 140-kilometre frontage covered two diverging directions: Kremenchuk–Romodan and Deriivka–Poltava. A single army headquarters was being asked to manage threats moving away from each other. The proposal identified formations for each sector and sought approval for a new army command. It was an effort to improve control, but reorganizing a headquarters during a breakthrough could not instantly restore the communications and reserves already missing. The document records an attempted solution whose execution still depended on time.[1]

New tanks, unfamiliar crews

When the 142nd Tank Brigade reached Poltava on 7 September, Budenny and Nikita Khrushchev inspected its readiness. Their report to Stalin complained that half the personnel in crews assigned to KV and T-34 tanks had not previously operated those machines. Some commanders had received their appointments during loading, and the antiaircraft gunners had not fired their weapons. These were criticisms in a contemporary headquarters report, not measurements independently taken by the historian. Even with that qualification, they explain why newly delivered equipment did not immediately equal experienced combat strength. The report recommended giving machines to tested formations that had lost their tanks instead of assembling new mixed units. Behind the brigade’s designation were men expected to learn unfamiliar equipment while moving toward an emergency. Their difficulty was a product of the replacement system as well as the enemy they were about to face.[1]

The decisions that left the armies exposed

Kirponos commanded the Southwestern Front, while Marshal Semyon Budenny’s Southwestern Direction coordinated a broader theatre. Above both stood Stalin and the Stavka, the supreme command. This hierarchy matters because a request from the front could be endorsed at the theatre level and still refused in Moscow. The surviving documents also prevent an oversimplified claim that every retreat was prohibited. On 9 September, the supreme command approved withdrawal of the 5th Army and the right flank of the 37th Army to the Desna, while explicitly requiring retention of the Kiev bridgehead and specified connecting positions. A limited adjustment was authorized within a strategy that continued to demand possession of Kiev.[1]

The central warning followed on 11 September. In report 0332, signed by Budenny, Khrushchev and chief of staff Alexander Pokrovsky, the Southwestern Direction told Stalin that the front’s military council wanted a general withdrawal. The report stated that Shaposhnikov, speaking for the Stavka, considered an eastward retreat premature and recommended using two divisions from the 26th Army against the breakthrough. Budenny’s response was explicit: the German intention to envelop the front from Novgorod-Seversky and Kremenchuk had become clear, and the front could not assemble a sufficiently strong force to prevent it.[1]

This was a contemporary warning, not merely a later memoir’s claim that someone had foreseen disaster. It also explained why moving two divisions did not solve the larger problem. Removing them would leave the 26th Army with only three rifle divisions across roughly 150 kilometres. The proposed reinforcement would therefore create weakness elsewhere, and it could at best cover a larger withdrawal rather than replace one. The report warned that delay might cost both troops and substantial equipment. As a fallback, it requested permission to remove at least the forces and resources of the Kiev fortified region. The distinction between this argument and an indiscriminate demand to abandon all resistance is important: withdrawal was proposed as a means of preserving an army capable of continuing the war.

Orders issued on 12 September show what happened instead. At 08.35, the front instructed the 26th Army to get the 289th Rifle Division and 7th Motorised Rifle Division to loading stations as quickly as possible. Personal responsibility was placed on the army commander for their concentration and dispatch. The urgency was unmistakable, but the divisions still had to be disengaged, assembled and loaded. Kirponos’s appeal for a tank brigade later that afternoon acknowledged the interval before they could arrive. A headquarters could reassign a division in minutes; the troops and equipment remained subject to the physical sequence of a military movement.[1]

Communications were failing during these decisions. An order issued at 05.45 on 12 September reprimanded the 40th Army for two days without effective contact, including unsuccessful attempts to reach it by radio. Information was arriving late and no longer described the current situation. The front demanded regular reports. This was not a minor administrative complaint. Without knowing which roads remained open or which formations were still coherent, Kirponos could not reliably coordinate reinforcements or judge the speed of the German advance. The order also reveals a familiar feature of a collapsing front: as the need for information increased, the ability to provide it diminished.[1]

The immediate approaches to Kiev were also consuming reserves. On 12 September the 37th Army reported fighting around Kozelets and a German penetration between the 87th and 146th Rifle Divisions near Volchya Gora. Two battalions from the 147th Division were committed to meet that breakthrough. Farther south, the fortified region still resisted attacks. This uneven picture helps explain why an army commander could report continued defence of Kiev while the front commander saw the city’s position becoming untenable. Troops needed to repair a local breach were the same troops that might otherwise cover a withdrawal or reinforce the distant threatened flank. Every successful emergency response could leave the next emergency with fewer resources.[1]

Transport, labour and the people behind the front

The movement toward Romny exposed rear areas that had previously supported the defence along the Dnieper. Depots and transport services belonged to an arrangement designed around a different front. When German troops approached them from the side or rear, the problem was not simply that supplies ran out. Supplies could remain in places from which they could no longer reach their intended units. Ammunition of the wrong type, fuel separated from the vehicles that needed it, or a train unable to pass a threatened junction could have little immediate value. The 40th Army’s reported difficulty obtaining food and ammunition gives this general problem a contemporary setting.[1]

For the Germans, road conditions limited the rate at which a successful penetration could become a secure corridor. Guderian’s account describes difficult movement behind the Romny spearhead and interruptions to reconnaissance during bad weather. Those observations should not be expanded into a claim that the autumn mud season had already immobilized every sector. The relevant point is local and dated: early September rain impeded movement during this operation. Soviet reports of stalled wheeled transport near the Kremenchuk bridgehead provide independent evidence that the same period disrupted the opposing side’s plans. Weather did not choose a belligerent; its effects depended on where each force was moving and which vehicles its task required.[3][1]

Civilian labour had helped construct the positions now threatened with being outflanked. A report dated 7 August described extensive work on the Dnieper and on a rear line running through Bakhmach, Romny and Lubny. Construction battalions and local inhabitants were building gun positions, antitank obstacles and infantry defences. The figures in that report describe the earlier construction effort, not the number of civilians working on 12 September. They nevertheless establish that the landscape of the battle had been remade through labour drawn from the surrounding population. Losing a position meant losing the military value of that work as well as the ground itself.[1]

The same report identified shortages of wire, mines and fuzes. Locally made wooden antitank mine cases could not be issued without the necessary firing mechanisms. This detail exposes the limits of treating labour as an inexhaustible substitute for materials. People could dig and build, but an unfinished obstacle might lack the component that made it effective. The burden was also social. Time devoted to military construction came from households and communities already dealing with mobilisation and disruption. The documents count workers and completed positions; they do not record every family consequence. That silence should not remove civilian labour from an account of how the defence functioned.[1]

Transport decisions could transfer that burden from one system to another. An order of 20 August directed civilian vessels to unload cargo and continue its evacuation by land, while powered craft were to move toward Kiev under military protection. Craft without propulsion were to be placed in backwaters and prepared for destruction rather than left to the enemy. This was an earlier response to the deteriorating river situation, not a new order on 12 September. Its continuing relevance is that road and rail transport had already been asked to absorb work formerly performed on the river. By the time the pincers approached, the rear was not an untouched reserve of spare capacity.[1]

A new commander, an incomplete picture

Budenny was replaced by Semyon Timoshenko as the crisis intensified. The direct-wire conversation concluded shortly after midnight on 13 September records the incoming commander describing German tanks moving out of the Kremenchuk area and reports of a northern group approaching Lokhvytsia. These were headquarters assessments at that moment; the mention of Lokhvytsia should not be converted into a verified German junction there on 12 September. The conversation shows the Soviet leadership anticipating the convergence while still attempting to strike its separate arms. Timoshenko proposed moving cavalry and reinforcing it with tanks under repair in Kharkov, another attempt to turn resources that existed somewhere into forces available at the threatened point.[1]

Timoshenko’s arrival under air attack

Timoshenko began that conversation by saying that he had reached the area safely despite being bombed before arriving at Poltava. He then moved directly to the worsening operational position and the reserves he was trying to shift. The brief personal detail belongs to a contemporary communication, not a later scene reconstructed for dramatic effect. It shows that even a senior commander’s journey took place within the transport and air situation he was expected to control. It also places the transfer of authority in a moment of uncertainty: Timoshenko reported that he was learning the situation, while Budenny had not yet received all the instructions concerning the handover. A replacement at the top could alter decisions, but it did not erase the time needed to understand reports, locate formations and establish working relationships with a headquarters already under pressure.[1]

The British and Americans also saw danger through incomplete information. In a telegram of 13 September describing conversations on the previous evening, U.S. Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt reported that the British military representative in Moscow lacked reliable details about Soviet dispositions, losses and reserves. He nevertheless considered the situation on and east of the Dnieper serious. This was an informed observer acknowledging the limits of his knowledge, not a precise independent reconstruction of Kirponos’s front. Allied concern could be strong while the operational information available to support it remained fragmentary.[4]

Steinhardt also relayed Stafford Cripps’s discussion with Stalin about the possibility of a separate Soviet peace with Germany. Stalin assured the British ambassador that the Soviet Union would continue fighting even beyond the Volga if necessary. The assurance addressed the survival of the alliance, whereas Kirponos’s messages addressed the survival of particular armies. These were connected but distinct scales of decision. A government’s determination to continue the war did not make a threatened formation capable of escaping; the impending loss of that formation did not by itself prove that the government would abandon the war.[4]

Even senior Soviet officers did not always share the same inventory of reinforcements. During the overnight conversation, Shaposhnikov said he had understood that only two tank brigades were available after Timoshenko described allocations involving three. The correction was small in wording but large in consequence: different assumptions about one brigade could change which threatened direction a headquarters believed it had covered.[1]

The narrowing interval

David Stahel’s study of Kiev cautions against reading German operational success as evidence that the invading army had solved its strategic problems. That distinction is especially useful at this stage. The German forces were achieving a dangerous convergence while experiencing wear, supply difficulties and pressure on their flanks. Soviet command decisions enlarged the consequences of that success by leaving major formations exposed after the danger had been identified. These explanations reinforce rather than cancel one another. Recognising German limitations does not reduce the scale of the approaching Soviet defeat; recognising Soviet mistakes does not make German success effortless.[5]

An earlier general withdrawal would also have been an operation under enemy pressure, with losses and uncertainty of its own. The surviving warnings support the conclusion that delay worsened the danger; they do not allow an exact calculation of how many men or vehicles a different decision would have saved. The strongest judgment rests on what commanders knew and what they ordered. By 11–12 September, the encircling design had been explicitly described, the shortage of reserves acknowledged and the costs of holding the existing positions identified. Continuing to demand those positions consumed the remaining interval in which movement could have been organised before the ring closed.

On the chapter’s anchor date, that ring was still open. German troops were moving south from Romny and north from the Kremenchuk area, while Soviet headquarters tried to redirect divisions, restore communications and contain both threats. The next chapter, The Encirclement Closes, follows the junction and the struggle to turn a line of mobile detachments into a defended perimeter. The distinction matters: the trap was becoming decisive on 12 September, but the soldiers inside it had not yet lived through the attempts to close, hold or break it.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. Contemporary orders establish intentions, while reports contain the information, estimates and gaps known to their authors. Retrospective military accounts and testimony are identified and assessed alongside documentary evidence and scholarship. English paraphrases of Russian, Ukrainian and German texts are by the atlas unless a published translator is named. Archival references reproduced in published sources do not imply direct archival inspection. Events after the chapter date are dated explicitly. The companion map is a dated regional military reconstruction; its feature sources and precision notes distinguish reported positions from approximate connecting edges.
